🧠 THE SCIENCE
This Is a Wiring Difference, Not a Behavior Choice
The Communication Pathway
When a neurotypical child communicates, five steps fire in sequence: thought formation → word retrieval → sentence assembly → motor speech execution → listener comprehension.
In children with expressive challenges, one or more nodes process differently — creating the gap between the fully-formed thought and the successfully-received message.
The metacognitive skill of recognizing "my message didn't get through" requires self-monitoring circuits that are often underdeveloped. This is why children repeat the identical failed attempt — it's not stubbornness. It's a neurological gap.
Plain English Translation
Your child's brain is working hard. The thought is complete. The translation system has a bottleneck — like a traffic jam between what they know and what comes out.
"Use your words" doesn't work because the bottleneck isn't in motivation — it's in the neural pathway from thought to speech. Demanding the broken pathway work harder doesn't fix it. Building alternative pathways does.
What these 9 materials do: they create parallel communication highways — picture routes, gesture routes, technology routes — so when the speech highway jams, the message still arrives.
📅 DEVELOPMENTAL CONTEXT
Your Child's Journey on the Developmental Map
Communication breakdown is most intense between ages 2–7, when a child's receptive vocabulary dramatically outpaces expressive vocabulary, narrative demands increase at school, and social communication becomes more complex. This technique targets the exact gap between knowing and expressing.
Autism Spectrum Disorder
Pragmatic + expressive challenges
Childhood Apraxia of Speech
Motor speech difficulty
Developmental Language Disorder
Receptive/expressive gap
Expressive Language Disorder
Word retrieval and formulation

📖 THE TECHNIQUE
Building Communication Bridges When Words Fail
Technique Code B-219 | Domain B: Social Communication & Pragmatic Language
Communication breakdown occurs when a child's intended message fails to reach the listener — when the thought is complete but the delivery fails. This technique teaches children that when speech doesn't work, they have options: pictures, gestures, signs, technology, context-setting, simplification, or showing. By building a toolkit of 9 materials, we transform communication breakdown from a dead end into a detour.
🧩 Domain
B: Social Communication & Pragmatic Language
👤 Age Range
2–12 years core window, applicable beyond
⏱️ Duration
10–15 min | 3–5× daily in natural routines
📍 Settings
Home • School • Community • Anywhere

👥 WHO USES THIS
This Technique Lives at the Intersection of Five Disciplines
Speech-Language Pathologist (PRIMARY)
Leads AAC evaluation and implementation, repair strategy teaching, and intelligibility therapy. The SLP designs the communication system.
Occupational Therapist
Addresses sensory and regulatory foundations. When dysregulation triggers breakdown, OT-led strategies create the preconditions for repair.
BCBA / ABA Therapist
Structures reinforcement around successful communication attempts — any modality. Addresses communication-based behavior.
Special Educator
Ensures communication supports generalize to academic settings. Implements classroom-level systems and coordinates school communication.
NeuroDevelopmental Pediatrician
Identifies underlying diagnoses contributing to breakdown — ASD, DLD, apraxia, intellectual disability.
🎯 WHAT THIS TARGETS
Six Functional Targets. One Goal: Communication That Succeeds.
🎯 Target 1: Communication Repair Frequency
Child attempts at least one different communication strategy when not understood — versus repeating identically or giving up entirely.
🎯 Target 2: Repair Strategy Variety
Child uses 3+ different repair approaches across contexts: speech modification, gesture, picture, AAC, showing.
🎯 Target 3: Multimodal Communication
Child independently selects and uses an alternative modality (picture/sign/AAC) when speech fails.
🎯 Target 4: Frustration Tolerance
Child maintains regulatory baseline during communication failure — no meltdown or withdrawal — ≥70% of opportunities.
🎯 Target 5: Communication Initiation
Child does not withdraw from communication attempts due to anticipated failure — maintains initiation rate.
🎯 Target 6: Cross-Setting Generalization
Communication repair strategies used with unfamiliar partners, in school and community settings.

MATERIAL 1 OF 9
Communication Repair Strategy Cards
"What to try when the first attempt fails" | ₹200–800 | DIY: Free
Visual cards that explicitly teach children alternative strategies when their message doesn't get through. Each card shows one repair approach: Say it differently · Show me · Point to a picture · Use fewer words · Act it out · Give me context · Draw it.
The Repair Hierarchy — Teach in This Order
  1. Repeat with modification (slower, louder, clearer)
  1. Use fewer or simpler words
  1. Add a gesture or sign
  1. Show, point, or demonstrate
  1. Use a picture or AAC
  1. Set the context/topic first
  1. Break into smaller pieces
DIY Construction
Create A6-sized cards with the strategy name in large print, a simple illustration of the strategy in action, and "Try THIS when I don't understand" framing. Laminate for durability. Attach Velcro to a lanyard for portability.
Safety Note
Introduce and practice repair strategies when calm — not during breakdown. During breakdown, offer the card as a prompt. Gradually fade prompting as child internalizes the strategies.
"When children have only one way to communicate and it fails, they're stuck. Multiple repair strategies mean communication failure isn't the end — it's just the first try."
MATERIAL 2 OF 9
Picture Communication Boards & Books
"Point when words won't come" | ₹300–2,000 | DIY: Free–₹200
Visual displays showing pictures, symbols, or photographs that children can point to when spoken words fail. Core vocabulary boards include high-frequency, cross-context words: more, help, stop, want, like, don't like, yes, no, feelings, people, places, activities.
Why They Work
When speech is unintelligible or word-finding fails, pointing to a picture communicates with absolute clarity. Pictures don't depend on articulation, don't require word retrieval, and don't break down under emotional or cognitive load. For many children, having a picture backup paradoxically improves verbal attempts by reducing pressure.

Research-confirmed: Providing picture alternatives does NOT reduce speech attempts. It reduces frustration — and a less frustrated child tries harder.
Board Design Principles
  • Include core vocabulary (works across all contexts)
  • Include fringe vocabulary (child's specific interests)
  • Use photos of actual objects for young children
  • Organize by category for larger boards
  • Board travels with child — school bag, kitchen, car
DIY Option
Print from Boardmaker, Widgit, or free Mulberry symbols. Mount on cardstock, laminate, Velcro.
MATERIAL 3 OF 9
Choice Boards for Specific Situations
"Pick instead of produce" | ₹200–1,000 | DIY: Free
The Cognitive Load Science
There are two fundamentally different cognitive tasks:
Recall (production): "What do you want?" — child must retrieve word from memory, formulate phrase, execute speech. High cognitive load.
Recognition (selection): "Which one?" while showing options — child simply identifies the right picture. Low cognitive load.
For children whose expressive pathway is congested, reducing the task to recognition prevents breakdown before it starts.
6 Boards to Create First
  1. Kitchen board: snack/drink options (photographs)
  1. Playroom board: activity options
  1. Getting-dressed board: clothing choices
  1. Feelings board: emotion options
  1. Going out board: destination options
  1. Morning routine board: sequenced options
Key Design Rule: Always include "something else" or "none of these" — autonomy is non-negotiable.
MATERIAL 4 OF 9
Gesture & Sign Language Supports
"Another way to say it when words blur" | ₹0–1,500 | DIY: Free
Natural gestures and simple signs borrowed from Indian Sign Language (ISL) or ASL for high-frequency communication needs — used alongside speech, not instead of it.
MORE
HELP
STOP
WANT
FINISHED
DRINK
EAT
PLEASE
YES
NO

Research-confirmed across 47+ studies: Signs do NOT inhibit speech development. Children who sign alongside speech attempts show equal or greater speech development compared to speech-only approaches. All communication partners must learn the child's signs — consistency is the critical factor.
MATERIAL 5 OF 9
High-Tech AAC Devices & Apps
"Technology speaks when words can't" | Free apps → ₹1,50,000+ dedicated devices
Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) tools provide a voice output — the child selects symbols or words, and the device speaks the message aloud.
Three Categories of AAC
  1. Free apps (₹0): Cboard (open-source), LetMeTalk (free, Android), Communication Builder (free, iOS)
  1. Subscription apps (₹3,000–12,000/year): Proloquo2Go, TouchChat HD, LAMP Words for Life
  1. Dedicated devices (₹80,000–₹1,50,000+): Tobii Dynavox, Accent, NovaChat
3 AAC Myths — Busted
Myth: "AAC will stop my child from talking."
Fact: 47+ studies confirm AAC supports speech development, not replaces it.
Myth: "My child must fail at speech before trying AAC."
Fact: Early AAC prevents frustration and withdrawal.
Myth: "AAC is only for children who will never speak."
Fact: Many use AAC temporarily as speech develops.
AAC is not giving up on speech. AAC is giving your child a voice while speech develops.

📞9100 181 181 — Request formal AAC evaluation pathway | Device must be always available — removing AAC access is removing the child's voice
MATERIAL 6 OF 9
First-Then Boards & Visual Sequences
"Show the order of things when words scramble" | ₹200–800 | DIY: Free
Visual displays showing sequences of events, conditions, or multi-step messages. FIRST-THEN boards show two-step conditions. Extended sequence strips show morning routines, multi-step activities, or narrative events in picture order.
1
Morning Routine Strip
Wake → Breakfast → Teeth → Dress → Bag → School
2
First-Then Board
First: Homework → Then: iPad
3
Event Narrative Strip
What happened at school today — told in pictures
4
Transition Warning Board
5 more minutes → Finish time → Next activity
Visual sequences hold the structure together. The pictures don't disappear when the words do. The child can point to "FIRST this → THEN this" even when the sentence version disintegrates. DIY: Velcro-backed picture cards on a strip board.
MATERIAL 7 OF 9
Emotion & Feelings Charts
"Name what's happening inside when feelings have no words" | ₹100–600 | DIY: Free
Emotions are the most abstract communication task of all — converting an internal, invisible experience into a specific word and delivering it under the very conditions (distress, frustration, dysregulation) that most impair language production.
Why They Matter
When children cannot verbalize emotional state, behavior becomes the communication — meltdown = "I am overwhelmed and can't express it." Adults respond to the behavior, not the emotion, causing escalation.
A feelings chart makes the invisible visible. The child points to "frustrated." You now know. You can respond to the actual emotion. The meltdown that was building is addressed early.
Four Chart Levels
  • Level 1: 4 basics — happy, sad, angry, calm
  • Level 2: 8 emotions — add scared, excited, confused, frustrated
  • Level 3: Zones of Regulation full set
  • Level 4: Body-sensation-emotion map
Placement: Bedroom door, kitchen, classroom desk, backpack pocket.

All emotions are valid — never tell a child their pointed feeling is wrong. The goal is communication and understanding, not emotional correction.
MATERIAL 8 OF 9
Topic & Context Cards
"Set the stage so your words have a chance" | ₹100–400 | DIY: Free
Category cards that establish the topic domain before a child attempts verbal communication. Child selects: "I'm talking about: School / Home / Friends / TV / Something I want / Something that happened / Something I'm worried about."
The Linguistic Context Science
When a child with unclear speech attempts a message, listeners do two jobs simultaneously: decoding phonemes and constructing meaning. When the topic is known, the second job disappears. "I went to the pa—" is uninterpretable. "I'm talking about: school trip" + "I went to the pa—" = "park" understood.
Create These Topic Cards
  • At school today / Yesterday at school
  • At home / In my room
  • About [family member name]
  • Something I want
  • Something that happened
  • Something I'm worried / sad / happy about
  • About a show / movie / game I like

Use case during breakdown: "Wait — can you show me what this is about?" → offer topic cards → narrow the field → retry communication.
MATERIAL 9 OF 9
Calm-Down & Regulation Tools
"Regulate first, then try again" | ₹100–1,500 | DIY: ₹0–₹200
Why They Come Last — But Matter Most: Communication breakdown → frustration → dysregulation → offline language processing. When a child is dysregulated, Broca's area and the prefrontal cortex go offline. No picture board or AAC will work when the nervous system is in fight/flight. Regulation comes first.
Stress Ball / Putty
Proprioceptive input. ₹150–500
Breathing Card
"Smell the flower, blow out the candle" visual. DIY free.
"Break" Visual Card
Child can request regulation break independently.
Calm Corner
Designated space with comfort item. Free to create.
Movement Break Cards
Jumping, wall push, spinning. Proprioceptive reset.
Weighted Lap Pad
Proprioceptive calming. ₹800–2,500
"Regulation time is not punishment. Going to the calm corner is not a consequence. It is a skill — the skill of returning to the communicative state. Model it yourself."

🚦 SAFETY FIRST
Read Before Every Session
🟢 GREEN — PROCEED
  • Child is calm, alert, and rested
  • Child has recently eaten (not hunger-dysregulated)
  • Environment is quiet and low-stimulation
  • All communication partners understand the materials
  • You have 10–15 minutes of uninterrupted time
🟡 AMBER — MODIFY
  • Child is mildly dysregulated → start with calm-down tools first
  • Child is tired → shorten to 3–5 minutes, one material only
  • Environment is noisy → move to quieter space
  • Child shows mild resistance → use choice ("Which board today?")
🔴 RED — STOP
  • Child is in active meltdown → regulation first, no demands
  • Child has been ill or medically unwell → rest, not intervention
  • Child is showing self-injurious behavior → call 9100 181 181
  • Materials introduced too quickly → return to previous stage

AAC-Specific Safety Note: Removing or restricting a child's access to AAC is harmful. AAC is not a reward to be earned or withheld — it is the child's voice. 📞9100 181 181
🏠 PREPARE YOUR SPACE
Your Home Is Already the Right Setting. Here's How to Optimize It.
📍 Location Checklist
  • Quiet room with minimized background noise
  • Child's preferred, familiar space
  • Face-to-face positioning possible
  • Good lighting — child can see visual supports clearly
🗂️ Materials Prepared
  • Communication boards within reach (not packed away)
  • Repair strategy cards visible or accessible
  • Feelings chart on wall or in binder
  • Calm-down kit within arm's reach
📱 Technology
  • AAC device/app charged and loaded
  • Device within reach throughout activity (not put away)
  • Volume at comfortable level
🧩 The Golden Rule
Materials that are packed away don't help. Materials within reach — on walls, in bags, on the table — become part of life.
Embed into every natural routine. Breakfast = Choice board. Morning = Visual sequence. Before school = Feelings chart. AAC device at meals, school pick-up, play, bedtime.

STEP 1 OF 6
The Invitation
The Principle: Every communication session begins with an invitation, not a demand.
What to Say — Script
"Hey [child's name], I have something interesting to show you. Want to try this with me?"
For a child who communicates better visually:
[Show the picture board / repair card / AAC device]
"Look what we have. Can we try this together?"
Body Language
  • Get to child's eye level — floor or kneel
  • Relaxed posture, no tension or urgency
  • Warm, genuinely curious expression
  • Don't block exit — child should feel free to walk away
Acceptance Looks Like
  • Approaches or leans in
  • Eye contact or visual orientation to material
  • Reaching toward material
  • ANY positive vocalization or gesture
If Resistance
Do not pursue. Offer choice: "Should we try the picture board or the cards?" If still refusing — postpone 10–15 minutes. Never force the start.

ABA Pairing Principle: Every forced session damages future acceptance. The child must associate materials with positive experiences.
STEP 2 OF 6
Introduce the Material
🖼️ For Picture Boards
Place board between you and child. Point to one picture: "This picture means [drink]. If you want a drink, you can touch this." Immediately offer drink when child touches — even accidentally at first.
🃏 For Repair Strategy Cards
"When I don't understand you, you can try one of these." Show 2–3 cards only. Don't overwhelm with the full set at once.
📱 For AAC Device
Model first. Press a symbol yourself. "I pressed 'help'. That means 'help me.' Now you try." The adult models AAC before the child is expected to use it.
😊 For Feelings Chart
"Look at all these faces. This one is 'frustrated.' Can you show me which one you feel right now?" No wrong answers.
🤟 For Signs
"I'm going to teach you a secret signal. When you want MORE of something, you do this [demonstrate MORE sign]. Let's try it."

Reinforcement starts NOW: Any engagement with material → immediate warm praise. "Yes! You touched the picture!" Even looking at it = praiseworthy. Timing: 1–3 minutes.
STEP 3 OF 6
The Communication Repair Moment
This is the active ingredient of the entire session. Use real moments — at mealtime, during play, at snack — rather than manufactured stress.
The 4-Step Repair Cycle is your template for every natural breakdown moment. Set up opportunities by gently delaying response to see if child initiates with support, holding a preferred item just out of reach, or briefly pretending not to understand.
✅ DO
Accept ANY modality that successfully communicates the message. Stay calm — your calm IS the intervention. Target ≥70% breakdown-to-repair success rate.
❌ DON'T
Ask the child to "say it again" without offering a repair tool. Express frustration at breakdown. Guess repeatedly without narrowing with topic card.
STEP 4 OF 6
Repeat & Vary
Therapeutic Dosage Principle: 3 high-quality, successful repair cycles are more valuable than 10 prompted, pressured attempts.
Repetition Protocol
  • Target 3–5 natural communication repair opportunities per 10-minute session
  • Vary the situation — don't use the same breakdown scenario repeatedly
  • Rotate the repair tools so the child builds a repertoire, not a single habit
Vary Across These Dimensions
  • Motivation: snack → toy → activity → social game
  • Repair tool: picture board, sign, AAC, topic card
  • Communication partner: both parents, sibling, grandparent
  • Setting: kitchen → living room → outdoor
Satiation Indicators — When to Stop
  • Child pushes materials away
  • Child stops engaging with communication opportunity
  • Increased frustration without successful repair
  • Visible fatigue
The "3 Good Reps" Rule
If 3 successful repair cycles have happened within a 10-minute window — end the structured session there. Don't push for more. The neural pathways have been activated enough for today.

NCAEP 2020 recommends 3–5 sessions/week embedded in natural routines.
STEP 5 OF 6
Reinforce & Celebrate
ABA Principle: Timing matters more than magnitude. Deliver reinforcement within 3 seconds of the desired behavior.
"YES! You showed me [the picture]! I know what you mean! You want [X]! You told me!"
What to Reinforce
  • Reinforce the communication success — not the method: "You told me! I understood!"
  • Reinforce the repair ATTEMPT even if unsuccessful: "Great try — you used the picture!"
  • Do NOT withhold reinforcement pending "better" communication
Reinforcement Menu
  • Immediate access to requested item (most powerful)
  • Enthusiastic verbal praise: specific, immediate, genuine
  • Physical celebration: high five, hug if child tolerates
  • Token: sticker on chart (older children)
  • 2 minutes of favourite preferred activity

Celebrate the attempt, not just the success. Every child who tries a repair strategy — even unsuccessfully — is building the neural pathway. 📞 9100 181 181
STEP 6 OF 6
The Cool-Down
The Rule: No session ends abruptly. A predictable ending creates psychological safety for the next session — especially for children who have experienced repeated communication failure.
01
Advance Warning (2 min before end)
"Two more tries, then we're all done with our communication practice today." Show a visual timer or count down on fingers.
02
The Wrap-Up Communication
Ask one final, easy success-guaranteed question using the child's most reliable modality: "Can you show me on the feelings chart how you feel right now?"
03
Material Put-Away Ritual
Have the child help put materials away if able. Signals session closure AND reinforces that materials will return.
04
Transition Statement
"Great communicating today. You showed me / used the picture / used the sign. I'm so proud. Now let's [transition to preferred activity]."
05
Preferred Activity Transition
Immediately move to something the child enjoys — this creates a positive association with the end of communication practice.
📈 CAPTURE THE DATA
60 Seconds. 3 Data Points. This Is How Progress Becomes Visible.
Data captured today drives tomorrow's plan. Without records, you won't see gradual progress, your SLP cannot adjust the intervention, and the GPT-OS® cannot generate prognostic updates.
Quick Session Log
  • Materials used today: ___________
  • Number of communication breakdowns: ___
  • Number of successful repairs: ___
  • Repair strategies used: Picture / Sign / AAC / Gesture / Simplified / Showed
  • Frustration level (1–5): ___
  • Child's mood at end (feelings chart word): ___
  • Any new behavior observed: ___
GPT-OS® Integration
Session data feeds four live indexes:
  • Expressive Communication Readiness Index
  • Communication Repair Index
  • Functional Communication Index
  • TherapeuticAI® plan adjustment triggers

🔧 TROUBLESHOOTING
The Most Common Challenges — And What to Do
🔴 "My child refuses to use any of the materials"
Return to pairing — associate materials with pure positive experiences (no demands). Use materials during play with NO communication requirement first. Model yourself using picture boards and AAC throughout the day. Consult SLP: underlying sensory aversion possible.
🟠 "Child uses board at home but refuses at school"
Generalization issue — the school needs to implement the same system. Copy board for school. Gradual introduction in lowest-demand context first. Contact 9100 181 181 for school implementation support.
🟠 "Child picks the same strategy repeatedly and won't expand"
Normal developmental step — they're building confidence with one tool. Gently expand: "You used the picture. Can we also try the sign this time?" Add reinforcement for variety.
🟡 "Meltdowns haven't reduced even with all materials"
Assess regulatory foundation — is calm-down toolkit adequate? Review whether communication demands have actually decreased. May indicate need for direct SLP + OT collaboration. Call 9100 181 181.
🟢 "Progress seems very slow"
Communication repair is a long-term skill. Track repair ATTEMPTS, not just successful repairs. Even one more repair strategy than last month = real, measurable progress. Trust the timeline.
🎨 PERSONALISE
Every Child Is Different. Here's How to Tune the Approach.
Primarily Non-Verbal Child
Lead with AAC device + picture boards + signs from Day 1. De-emphasize verbal repair strategies temporarily. Build multimodal system before expecting verbal repair.
Partially Verbal / Intelligibility Challenges
Signs as speech clarifiers (sign + speech simultaneously). Picture boards as backup for unclear messages. Repair strategies focused on "add a sign" and "show me."
Verbally Fluent / Word-Finding Difficulties
Topic cards first (set the context). Visual sequence strips for narrative organization. Repair strategies focused on simplification and segmentation.
Emotionally Dysregulated Child
Regulation toolkit as prerequisite — master calm-down first. Feelings chart as primary entry point. Short sessions (3–5 minutes) with long recovery periods.
Age-Based Modifications
  • Ages 2–4: Photographs over symbols, 2–4 item boards, gestural emphasis, parent-mediates all
  • Ages 4–7: Symbol-based systems, 6–9 item boards, signs + AAC introduction
  • Ages 7–12: Full repair strategy card sets, narrative visual supports, self-advocacy language
Bilingual / Multilingual Families
Materials can be in any language or combination. Create boards in the child's home language. Sign vocabulary in ISL (Indian Sign Language). AAC apps support multiple Indian languages.
📈 ACT IV — PROGRESS ARC
Weeks 1–2: Building the Foundation
✅ What You WILL See
  • Child tolerates materials being present (even if not using them)
  • Some eye contact with picture board or repair card when offered
  • Parent gains confidence in how to present materials and respond
  • One or two moments where a material successfully bridged the gap
  • Baseline frustration level established
🔶 What You Might See
  • Initial resistance or indifference to new materials
  • Meltdowns continuing at roughly the same frequency (normal — change takes time)
  • Child using ONE familiar material only
❌ Not Yet Expected
  • Spontaneous, independent use of repair strategies
  • Significant meltdown reduction
  • Consistent use of multiple modalities
"If your child tolerates a communication support material for even 10 seconds longer than the first time you introduced it — that's real, measurable progress."

📞9100 181 181 — Check in if you're struggling in Weeks 1–2. Week 1–2 is often the hardest. The neural pathways for repair are forming. Trust the process.
WEEKS 3–4
Weeks 3–4: Consolidation Signs
Neural pathways are forming. Watch for these early consolidation indicators — they are real evidence of neurological change, even when the improvements seem small.
🌱 Child reaches for repair card or picture board spontaneously
First signs of independent strategy selection — the self-monitoring circuit is activating.
🌱 Same repair strategy used more than once across different situations
Generalization beginning — the skill is moving from prompted to internalized.
🧠 Child pauses slightly before repeating the failed attempt
Self-monitoring system activating. This pause is a significant neurodevelopmental event.
📈 You're responding faster to communication breakdown
Your own repair strategy competence is growing — a critical variable in outcomes.

When to increase: If child is using ONE tool reliably → introduce second tool. If frequency ≥5 successful repairs/day → increase complexity of materials.
WEEKS 5–8
Weeks 5–8: Mastery Phase
🏆 Communication Repair Mastery
  • Child independently attempts a different strategy when first attempt fails (without prompting)
  • 2+ different repair modalities in regular use
  • Communication initiation rate has increased — child attempting MORE, not less
  • Meltdowns linked to communication frustration reduced by >30%
🌟 Generalization Mastery
  • Repair strategies appear in new, untrained settings
  • Child uses materials at school, with grandparents, in community
  • Child begins requesting their communication supports ("give me the book")
🔬 GPT-OS® AbilityScore® at 8 Weeks
  • Communication Repair Index: Emerging → Developing
  • Functional Communication Index: Baseline → Early improvement
  • Frustration Tolerance Index: Significant reduction in escalations
The first time your child reaches for the picture board instead of melting down — that is a neurodevelopmental achievement worth celebrating.

🚩 RED FLAGS
Home Intervention Has Limits. Know When to Escalate.
Contact 9100 181 181 immediately if any of the following apply:
🚩 Regression
Child was using a communication strategy reliably and has stopped completely for more than 1 week without explanation.
🚩 No Progress After 8 Weeks
Despite consistent use of materials 3–5 times daily, no measurable increase in repair attempts, modality use, or frustration tolerance.
🚩 Increasing Aggression or Self-Injury
Behavior intensity around communication failure is increasing, not decreasing.
🚩 Complete Communication Withdrawal
Child has stopped attempting to communicate in any modality with anyone.
🚩 Suspected Medical Cause
New or sudden communication changes — possible hearing loss or neurological changes. Seek immediate medical evaluation.
🚩 AAC Needed But Not Yet Evaluated
Child's speech unintelligibility is severe and no professional AAC assessment has occurred.
